author: Venkata varun Yelika, open to work
text:
Everyone is talking about AI. Very few are building AI employees.

Last week, I spoke with the founder of a fast-growing SaaS company.
 
He didn't ask:
 
❌ "Which LLM is the best?"
 
❌ "Should I use ChatGPT or Claude?"
 
His question was different.

"How do I build an AI employee that works 24/7 without hiring another team?"

That single question explains where the world is heading.

Companies are no longer looking for people who can use ChatGPT.
 
They're hiring people who can build systems that can:
 
✓ Understand business goals
 
✓ Make decisions
 
✓ Call APIs
 
✓ Search knowledge bases
 
✓ Automate workflows
 
✓ Collaborate with other AI agents
 
✓ Learn from previous interactions
 
✓ Deliver measurable business outcomes
 
Welcome to the era of Agentic AI.

Not AI chatbots.
 
Not prompt engineering.

Autonomous AI systems that execute real work.

Here's what's happening right now:
🏦 Banks are deploying AI agents for customer onboarding.
🏥 Healthcare organizations are building AI assistants that reduce documentation time.
🛍️ E-commerce companies use AI agents to manage inventory, customer support, and personalized recommendations.
🏢 Enterprises are replacing repetitive operations with AI workflows that run around the clock.
🏠 Real estate companies are building AI agents that qualify leads, answer property queries, schedule site visits, and follow up automatically.
The question is no longer:
"Will AI replace jobs?"
The real question is:
Who will build the AI workforce?

That's exactly why I created this Agentic AI Training Program.
This isn't another course that teaches prompts.
You'll build production-ready AI agents that businesses can actually deploy.
What you'll build:
✅ AI Sales Agents
✅ AI Customer Support Agents
✅ AI Research Agents
✅ AI Recruitment Agents
✅ Multi-Agent Systems
✅ RAG Applications
✅ MCP Integrations
✅ AI Workflow Automation
✅ Production Deployments

Technologies you'll work with
• Python
• LangGraph
• LangChain
• OpenAI
• MCP (Model Context Protocol)
• Vector Databases
• RAG
• n8n Automation
• APIs
• Production Deployment
• Monitoring & Evaluation

By the end, you'll have a portfolio that demonstrates production-ready AI engineering skills.

Who should join?
✔ Software Engineers
✔ AI/ML Engineers
✔ Data Engineers
✔ Founders
✔ Automation Consultants
✔ Students preparing for AI careers
✔ Anyone who wants to become an AI Agent Engineer before the market becomes saturated

The next decade won't be defined by people who know AI.
It will be defined by people who know how to build autonomous AI systems that create business value.
The demand has already started.
The supply is still very small.
That gap is your opportunity.

author: Ben Schwartz
text:
One project I recently wrapped up changed how I think about building AI systems.

I joined to help architect and build an enterprise ML platform focused on real-time inference. Leading the engineering effort gave me a front-row seat to the challenges that don't show up in architecture diagrams.

Going in, I assumed the hardest problems would be technical:

Low latency.
Scalable inference.
Reliable deployments.
Production monitoring.

Those were all challenging, but they weren't what consumed most of our time.

The harder conversations sounded more like this:

"Where does the platform team's responsibility end?"
"Where does backend engineering take over?"
"Who owns the model once it reaches production?"
"What guarantees should each team make to the teams that depend on them?"

At first glance, those sound like organizational questions. They're actually architectural decisions.

One of the biggest lessons I took away from the project is that unclear ownership creates technical bottlenecks. When the contracts between teams are blurry, every new model becomes a negotiation instead of an engineering task.

The fastest unblocker often isn't another engineer or another piece of infrastructure. It's defining clear interfaces between teams:

What does the platform team own?
What does backend engineering own?
What does data science own?
What can each team rely on without another meeting or Slack thread?

Once those boundaries are clear, teams move faster. Deployments become more predictable. Data scientists can iterate independently. Backend teams can build against stable interfaces instead of changing implementations.

As AI engineering continues to mature, I think this is one of the biggest shifts we'll see in hiring as well.

The conversation is gradually moving away from "We need an ML Engineer" or "We need a Data Scientist" and toward a more important question:

"What's actually preventing us from shipping AI?"

Sometimes it's the models.
Sometimes it's the platform.
Sometimes it's the architecture.
Sometimes it's simply that ownership was never clearly defined.

Those are four different problems. Hiring one person and hoping they solve all four rarely works.

The best AI teams won't necessarily be the ones with the biggest budgets or the most impressive tech stack. They'll be the ones that build systems and organizations with clear ownership, well-defined interfaces, and the ability to evolve without constantly getting in each other's way.

Curious if others building production AI have found the same thing.
